title: The cloud of unknowing
hook: an unnamed English monk: God is reached by love, not by thinking

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Laudato si', Francis's song: brother sun, sister water, even sister death. Your line was praised be, for sister water.

Some things you can't think your way into. You can read every book on swimming and still sink the first time you're in the deep end. You can analyze a piece of music bar by bar and never be moved by it. You can list everything you know about someone you love, and the list is not the love. Sometime in the late 1300s, an English writer whose name we'll never know wrote a small book arguing that God is like that. Not a problem to be solved. Someone to be reached, and not by the mind. Today: centering prayer.
screen: `BOOKS ON SWIMMING.` → `THE LIST IS NOT THE LOVE.` → `AN UNNAMED WRITER.`

segments.voice: The Cloud of Unknowing was written in Middle English, the English of Chaucer, probably by a priest or monk, maybe a Carthusian. Nobody knows. It's advice to a younger person who wanted to pray more deeply. Here's his picture. When you turn to God in prayer, you find something like a darkness between you and God. A cloud. Your mind can't see through it; you'll never figure God out. That's the cloud of unknowing. Everything else, even good thoughts, even holy thoughts, you put behind you, under a second cloud, a cloud of forgetting. So you sit between two clouds. Then what? You can't think your way through the cloud above, he says, but you can love your way through it. He pictures love as a sharp dart of longing, aimed up at the cloud. Beat on it with that longing love, and don't give up. In his own old English, God may well be loved, but not thought. By love he can be reached and held; by thinking, never. His practical advice is lovely. Take a short word, one syllable is best, like God, or love. Fasten it to your heart. When thoughts come crowding in, even clever ones, answer them with that one word and let them drop under the cloud of forgetting. You may recognize this from the desert: another way of staying in the cell. In the twentieth century, some Catholic monks drew on this book to teach a way of silent prayer many Christians now call centering prayer.
screen: `AN UNKNOWN WRITER, MIDDLE ENGLISH.` · `A CLOUD ABOVE, A CLOUD BEHIND.` · `A SHARP DART OF LONGING LOVE.` · `ONE SHORT WORD.`

segments.voice: Choose a short word, God, or love, or peace, and let it rest in you without thinking about what it means. When a thought arrives, a plan, a worry, even a good idea, don't fight it; return to your word, gently, and let the thought slip behind you. Again and again: that's the whole practice.
Centering prayer. The modern practice drawn from this book: using one short word to let go of thoughts and rest in God's presence.
Your line: reached by love. The mind stops at the cloud; love goes through. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Christians practice a form of silent prayer drawn from The Cloud of Unknowing, often called centering prayer, sitting for twenty minutes or so with a single sacred word.

fork.setup: you're praying, and a brilliant, holy thought arrives. what does the Cloud's author tell you to do with it?
options: let it drop under the cloud of forgetting.
fork.reveal: even good thoughts go under the cloud of forgetting. only the dart of longing love goes up.

trapdoor: what you thought: unknowing means being ignorant about God.
what it means: God is beyond what the mind can grasp, but love can reach where thinking can't.
what a scholar hears: an anonymous late fourteenth-century Middle English text, heir to Pseudo-Dionysius's 'mystical theology', and a source for modern centering prayer.

notes: All of the Cloud is paraphrased (no validator-listed translation). Chapter numbers: cloud of unknowing and dart of longing love (ch. 3, 6), cloud of forgetting (ch. 5), the short word (ch. 7), one-syllable prayer (ch. 37–39). Confirm.
